situationBrief.title: The Case of the Mismatched Verbs
situationBrief.description: Mira, Arjun, and Gyan are checking school club reports and event posters. Words squeezed between the Subject and verb are tricking students into picking the wrong verb!

storyIntro.previewSectionTitle: Clues pinned to the detective board
scatteredFragments: The basket of ripe mangoes are ...

beats.speaker: mira
beats.dialogue: Look at this school kitchen notice: 'The basket of ripe mangoes are fresh.' Why did someone write 'are' when there is only ONE basket?

beats.speaker: arjun
beats.dialogue: Wait—look at these slips too! 'Mathematics are fun', 'Each of the runners were fast', and 'Neither Ravi nor his friends is here.' How do we spot the real Subject every time?
beats.cardPreviewText: The basket of ripe mangoes are fresh.

beats.speaker: gyan
beats.dialogue: A finite verb must match the TRUE Subject head-word in Number and Person—never the nearby nouns in between! Grab your magnifying glass and solve all six clues!

grammarOutcomes: Lock finite verbs to the true Subject head-noun in Number (singular/plural) and Person, ignoring intervening 'of'-phrases.
Distinguish compound plural Subjects ('Mira and Arjun are') from single-idea pairs ('Rice and dal is') and one-determiner titles.
Apply concord rules accurately for 'with / as well as', 'either...or / neither...nor', plural-form singular nouns ('Mathematics'), 'police/cattle', and 'each of / neither of'.
learningObjectives.knowledgeOutcome: Audit school sports logs, healthy mid-day meal posters, and library invitations like a sharp Grammar Detective.

sourceReferences.bookTitle: A Practice Book of ENGLISH GRAMMAR & COMPOSITION (GRAMMAR IN USE) for Class IX

sentences.title: Clue 1: Intervening 'of'-Phrase Trap
sentences.rawText: The basket of ripe mangoes is on the table.
sentences.note: Ignore the prepositional phrase 'of ripe mangoes': the real Subject head-noun is singular 'basket'.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Names the one container—this word controls the verb!
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Singular head-noun of the Subject; takes singular verb 'is'.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Begins a describing phrase inside the Subject.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Prepositional phrases like 'of ripe mangoes' NEVER control the verb!
Part of the intervening phrase 'of ripe mangoes'.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Plural noun, but NOT the Subject head!
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Object of preposition 'of'—cannot decide the verb.

verbMeta.whyAppropriate: Only ONE basket is on the table; 'of ripe mangoes' is just an intervening modifier.

groups.label: Subject
groups.plainExplanation: 'basket' is the singular head-noun; 'of ripe mangoes' describes it.
groups.textbookRule: When a noun/pronoun is joined to other words by a preposition ('of', 'in'), the verb agrees with the FIRST/head Subject noun (PSEB IX p. 97).

groups.label: Predicate
groups.plainExplanation: 'is on the table' agrees with singular 'basket'.

relationships.label: is ← basket
relationships.explanation: 'is' locks directly to singular 'basket', skipping over 'of ripe mangoes'.

structureSummary.patternNote: Singular head ('basket') + intervening plural ('mangoes') → singular verb 'is'.

sentences.title: Clue 2: Single-Idea Pair With 'and'
sentences.rawText: Rice and dal is a wholesome meal.
sentences.note: Two nouns joined by 'and' normally take a plural verb, EXCEPT when they express ONE single meal or idea.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Combined with dal as one dish.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Together with 'and dal', expresses one single meal.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Joins two items into one meal.
Served together with rice as one meal.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Completes the single notion 'Rice and dal'.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Treats 'Rice and dal' as one wholesome meal.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Singular verb for a single-idea pair.

verbMeta.whyAppropriate: Two items forming one combined meal/notion ('rice and dal', 'slow and steady') take a singular verb.

tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Singular article 'a' confirms the single-idea reading.

groups.label: Subject
groups.questionPrompt: Are these two separate things or one meal?
groups.plainExplanation: 'Rice and dal' names one single meal.
groups.textbookRule: When two nouns joined by 'and' suggest one single idea or dish, they take a singular verb (PSEB IX p. 98; Assam p. 201).

groups.label: Predicate
groups.textbookRule: Compare: 'Mira and Arjun ARE teammates' (two people) vs 'Rice and dal IS a wholesome meal' (one dish).

structureSummary.patternNote: Two nouns expressing ONE combined idea → singular verb ('is').

sentences.title: Clue 3: Neither...Nor Nearest Subject
sentences.rawText: Neither the captain nor the players were late.
sentences.note: With 'either...or' or 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the NEARER subject ('players').

tokens.meaningInSentence: First subject, further from the verb.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Do not match the verb to 'captain' when 'players' is nearer.
Look right after 'nor' for the controlling noun.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Closest noun to the verb—controls agreement!
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Plural noun nearest to the verb requires plural 'were'.
Plural verb agreed with nearer noun.

verbMeta.whyAppropriate: With 'neither...nor', always place the plural noun nearer the verb and lock the verb to that nearer subject ('players → were').

groups.label: Subject
groups.questionPrompt: Which noun sits closest to the verb?
groups.plainExplanation: 'players' (plural) sits right next to the verb.
groups.textbookRule: When one subject is singular and the other plural joined by 'either...or / neither...nor', place the plural subject nearer and use a plural verb; when both differ in person, match the nearer one (PSEB IX p. 98).

relationships.label: were ← players
relationships.explanation: 'were' agrees with the nearer plural Subject 'players'.

structureSummary.subjectText: Neither the captain nor the players
structureSummary.patternNote: Contrast 'with / as well as' (FIRST subject wins) vs 'neither...nor' (NEARER subject wins).

sentences.title: Clue 4: 'Each of / Neither of' & '-s' Singulars
sentences.rawText: Each of the students has a library card.
sentences.note: Words like 'each', 'every', 'everyone', 'one of', and 'neither of' select ONE individual at a time, taking a singular verb.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Means every single student considered one by one.

verbMeta.whyAppropriate: 'Each of + plural noun' always focuses on one person at a time, so use singular 'has'.

groups.label: Subject
groups.plainExplanation: 'Each' is singular, even though 'students' is plural.
groups.textbookRule: 'Each, every, either, neither, everyone, one of + plural noun' take a singular verb formally (PSEB IX p. 99; Assam pp. 66-67).

relationships.label: has ← Each
relationships.explanation: 'has' locks onto singular 'Each', ignoring 'of the students'.

structureSummary.patternNote: 'Each / Every / One of / Neither of' + plural noun → formal singular verb.

teachingSequence.title: Rule 1: Number & Person Lock
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: A finite verb locks onto the true Subject head-noun—never nearby trap words!
teachingSequence.explanation: Every detective begins here: find the TRUE Subject head-noun and lock the verb to its Number (singular vs plural) and Person. In 'The basket of ripe mangoes is on the table', 'of ripe mangoes' is just extra description—the real Subject is ONE 'basket', so the verb is 'is'!

agreementData.ruleSummary: Ignore prepositional phrases ('of...', 'in...', 'from...') between Subject head and verb.
agreementData.contrastIncorrectText: The basket of ripe mangoes are on the table.
agreementData.contrastReason: 'mangoes' sits inside 'of ripe mangoes' and cannot control the verb.

teachingSequence.title: Rule 2: Intervening Phrases Trap
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: Cross out 'of...' or 'with...' in your mind to hear the true Subject + Verb pair.
teachingSequence.explanation: Try covering 'of ripe mangoes' with your finger: 'The basket ... is on the table' sounds right immediately! This trick also works with 'The quality of these apples is good' and 'The captain, with his teammates, was cheered'.

agreementData.ruleSummary: With 'with', 'as well as', or 'together with', the FIRST Subject controls the verb: 'The teacher, as well as the students, is happy.'

teachingSequence.title: Rule 3: Compound 'and' vs Single Idea
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: Two separate things ('Mira and Arjun are') vs one combined idea ('Rice and dal is').
teachingSequence.explanation: Normally, 'and' adds two Subjects together into a plural ('Mira and Arjun ARE teammates'). But when a traditional pair expresses ONE single meal or idea—like 'Rice and dal is a wholesome meal' or 'Slow and steady wins the race'—use a singular verb!

agreementData.ruleSummary: Also note one determiner = one person ('The poet and singer IS here'), whereas two determiners = two people ('The poet and the singer ARE here').
agreementData.contrastIncorrectText: Rice and dal are a wholesome meal.
agreementData.contrastReason: Notice 'a wholesome meal'—one singular meal calls for 'is'.

teachingSequence.title: Rule 4: Either...Or & Neither...Nor
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: With 'or / nor', the verb locks onto the subject closest to it!
teachingSequence.explanation: Compare joiners carefully: 'with / as well as' follows the FIRST subject, whereas 'either...or' and 'neither...nor' follow the NEAREST subject! Here, plural 'players' stands right before the verb, so we choose 'were'.

agreementData.ruleSummary: When subjects of different number/person join with 'either...or / neither...nor', place the plural subject closer and match the nearest subject.

teachingSequence.title: Rule 5: 'Each / Every / One of / Neither of'
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: Even before 'of the students', 'Each / Everyone / Neither of' takes a singular verb formally.
teachingSequence.explanation: Detectives watch for words ending or starting with one/each: 'Each of the students has', 'One of my friends lives', 'Neither of the answers is correct'. Always test 'Each ... has' rather than getting fooled by 'students'!

agreementData.ruleSummary: Formal grammar strictly requires a singular verb with 'each of / one of / neither of / either of'.
agreementData.contrastIncorrectText: Each of the students have a library card.
agreementData.contrastReason: 'Each' refers to one student at a time, so singular 'has' is required.
agreementData.informalUsageNote: Plural verbs sometimes appear after 'neither of / none of' in casual speech, but standard formal grammar expects the singular verb.

teachingSequence.title: Rule 6: '-s' Singulars vs Always-Plural Nouns
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: 'Mathematics IS' (one subject), while 'police / cattle ARE' and 'a pair of scissors IS'!
teachingSequence.explanation: Don't judge by '-s' alone! Subjects/news ending in '-s' ('Mathematics', 'Physics', 'news') are SINGULAR ('Mathematics is fascinating'). Meanwhile, 'police', 'people', and 'cattle' have no '-s' yet take PLURAL verbs ('The police have arrived'). And 'My scissors are sharp' vs 'A pair of scissors is on the desk'!

agreementData.ruleSummary: Also remember unit sums ('Ten kilometres IS a long walk') and preparatory 'there' ('There ARE forty desks' vs 'There IS a clock').

teachingSequence.title: Rule 7: Preparatory 'There' & Unit Quantities
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: With 'There is / There are', look AFTER the verb to find the real Subject!
teachingSequence.explanation: In 'There are twenty benches in the room', 'There' is only an introducer—the real Subject 'twenty benches' sits after the verb! Meanwhile, plural amounts seen as ONE whole unit—'Five hundred rupees is enough' or 'Ten kilometres is a long walk'—take a singular verb.

agreementData.subjectNumberPerson: Check actual noun or whole unit
agreementData.ruleSummary: 'There IS a neem tree' (singular) vs 'There ARE five neem trees' (plural); 'Ten kilometres IS a good morning walk' (one single distance).

teachingSequence.title: Inspect Concord Links Before Detective Lab
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: Tap 'Each', 'students', or 'has' above to see the lock note, then enter Guided Practice.
teachingSequence.explanation: Tap any word above to inspect its role and Subject-Verb lock. When ready, head into the Grammar Detective Lab to catch every verb trap!

wordLabActivities.title: A. Tap the True Controlling Subject Head
wordLabActivities.instruction: Ignore the 'of'-phrase! Tap ONLY the ONE word that controls the verb.
wordLabActivities.incorrectTitle: Don't get fooled by the noun inside the 'of'-phrase!

sentence.title: Detective Clue A
sentence.rawText: The quality of these fresh mangoes is wonderful.

structureSummary.subjectText: The quality of these fresh mangoes

wordLabActivities.correctFeedback: Sharp detective work! 'quality' (singular) controls 'is', even though 'mangoes' is plural.
wordLabActivities.incorrectFeedback: Tap ONLY the single head-noun before 'of' that controls 'is'.
wordLabActivities.hint: Ask: What IS wonderful—the mangoes or their quality?

wordLabActivities.title: B. Sort Subjects Into Singular Verb vs Plural Verb
wordLabActivities.instruction: Tap each Subject card, then sort whether it takes a Singular Verb (is/was/has) or Plural Verb (are/were/have).
wordLabActivities.promptText: 1. Tap a Subject card below, then tap Singular Verb or Plural Verb:

items.explanation: Subject names ending in '-s' take singular verbs.
Two distinct people joined by 'and' take a plural verb.

wordLabActivities.completeFeedback: Every tricky Subject sorted with zero traps missed!
wordLabActivities.incorrectFeedback: Watch out for '-s' singulars ('Mathematics'), 'a pair of', and always-plural nouns ('police', 'cattle'). Tap marked cards to move them.

wordLabActivities.title: C. Assemble an 'As Well As' Sentence
wordLabActivities.instruction: Arrange the tiles so the verb agrees with the FIRST subject ('The coach'), ignoring 'as well as the players'.
wordLabActivities.promptContext: 'as well as' keeps focus on the first Subject.
wordLabActivities.subjectText: The coach, as well as the players,
wordLabActivities.correctFeedback: Exact! Phrases introduced by 'with / as well as' do not make a singular Subject plural.
wordLabActivities.incorrectFeedback: Order: 'The coach,' + 'as well as' + 'the players,' + 'is' + 'ready for practice.'

wordLabActivities.title: D. Swap One Determiner, Flip the Verb!
wordLabActivities.instruction: Tap both options to see how repeating 'the' turns one person into two people.

options.meaningEffect: ONE determiner ('The') means ONE person holding both posts → singular 'is'.
TWO determiners ('The ... and the ...') mean TWO separate people → plural 'are'.

wordLabActivities.takeaway: One 'the' = one person ('is'); two 'the's = two distinct people ('are')!

wordLabActivities.title: E. Complete the Neither...Nor Invitation
wordLabActivities.instruction: Look closely at the subject closest to the blank and pick the matching verb.

options.feedback: 'Arjun' is singular, but 'his cousins' (plural) is closer to the blank and controls the verb!
Spot on! With 'neither...nor', plural 'his cousins' is nearer the verb, taking 'have'.
'is' does not form Present Perfect with 'visited', and 'his cousins' is plural.

wordLabActivities.title: F. Diagnose the Distance & Indefinite Trap
wordLabActivities.instruction: Read the flawed school sports card and select the accurate fix.
wordLabActivities.brokenSentence: Ten kilometres are a long distance to walk without water.
wordLabActivities.repairedSentence: Ten kilometres is a long distance to walk without water.
wordLabActivities.question: Why should 'are' change to 'is' here?

options.label: 'Ten kilometres' is treated as ONE single total distance, so it takes singular 'is'.
options.feedback: Accurate diagnosis! Sums of money, distances, and weights viewed as one whole take a singular verb.

options.label: 'kilometres' has an '-s', so it must stay 'are'.
options.feedback: Even though 'kilometres' ends in '-s', the whole phrase names one single distance ('a long distance').

options.label: Nothing is wrong; numbers larger than one always take 'are'.
options.feedback: Unit totals like 'Ten kilometres' and 'Five hundred rupees' take singular verbs when treated as one amount.

independentPractice.cueText: Tap the ONE true Subject head-noun before selecting the matching verb.
independentPractice.title: Challenge 1: Spot the Head-Noun Past the Trap
independentPractice.instruction: Ignore the 'of'-phrase, tap the real Subject word, then choose the right verb.
independentPractice.targetPrompt: Step 1: Tap the single head-noun that controls the verb

sentence.title: Independent Check 1
sentence.rawText: A bunch of fresh yellow bananas [?] on the kitchen shelf.

structureSummary.subjectText: A bunch of fresh yellow bananas

independentPractice.imperativeQuestion: Step 2: Which verb completes the sentence?

imperativeOptions.label: is
imperativeOptions.feedback: Exact! Singular 'bunch' locks the verb to 'is'.

imperativeOptions.label: are
imperativeOptions.feedback: Watch out—'bananas' is inside 'of fresh yellow bananas'; 'A bunch' is singular.

imperativeOptions.label: were
imperativeOptions.feedback: 'were' is plural, whereas 'A bunch' is singular.

independentPractice.cueText: Remember: 'Each boy and each girl...' repeats 'each'!
independentPractice.title: Challenge 2: 'Each' & 'Every' Rule
independentPractice.instruction: Select the verb that fits 'Each boy and each girl'.

sentence.title: Independent Check 2
sentence.rawText: Each boy and each girl in the choir _____ given a certificate.

structureSummary.subjectText: Each boy and each girl in the choir

independentPractice.imperativeQuestion: Which verb completes the sentence accurately?

imperativeOptions.label: were
imperativeOptions.feedback: Even though 'and' joins two nouns, 'Each' keeps the Subject singular!

imperativeOptions.label: was
imperativeOptions.feedback: Spot on! In 'Each boy and each girl was given a prize', 'each' or 'every' makes the Subject singular.

imperativeOptions.label: are
imperativeOptions.feedback: 'are' is plural, whereas 'Each' takes a singular verb.

independentPractice.successFeedback: 'Each' and 'Every' always call for a singular verb.

independentPractice.title: Challenge 3: Unfamiliar Case Audit
independentPractice.instruction: Find the ONE sentence with zero Subject–Verb Agreement errors.

sentence.title: Independent Check 3
sentence.rawText: Which school notice is grammatically correct?

imperativeOptions.label: One of the eco-club members water the garden every morning.
imperativeOptions.feedback: 'One' is singular, so the verb needs '-s' ('waters').

imperativeOptions.label: One of the eco-club members waters the garden every morning.
imperativeOptions.feedback: Correct! 'One (of the members)' is singular, locking onto 'waters'.

imperativeOptions.label: The news about tomorrow's solar fair are exciting.
imperativeOptions.feedback: 'news' ends in '-s' but is always singular ('is exciting').

independentPractice.successFeedback: Case closed! You solved all three detective challenges on your own.

completionSummary.headline: Case Solved! Lesson Complete!
completionSummary.celebrationMessage: You helped Mira, Arjun, and Gyan lock every Subject head-noun to its true verb!
learnedPoints: Finite verbs agree with the TRUE Subject head-word in Number and Person, ignoring prepositional phrases like 'of ripe mangoes'.
Normal 'and' pairs are plural, while single-idea pairs ('Rice and dal is') and single-determiner titles take singular verbs.

'with / as well as' follows the FIRST subject; 'either...or / neither...nor' follows the NEAREST subject; 'each / one of / neither of' and '-s' subjects like 'Mathematics / news' take singular verbs formally.

Rice and dal is a wholesome meal.
Neither the captain nor the players were late.
Each of the students has a library card.
